solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Harry Bishop breaks plates

indicators.note: the bishop's letters break into the word for plates, splitting it open in the middle

parts.note: plates of meat is rhyming slang for feet, so plates are FEET
RR, Right Reverend, is the title abbreviation for a bishop

explanation.surface: A clumsy cleric called Harry smashes the crockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' is the container signal. Plates = feet is Cockney rhyming slang, from 'plates of meat'; Harry is a verb, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry and to ferret are both verbs for pestering or hounding someone persistently.

clue.text: Down to reserve parliamentary report

parts.note: feeling down means feeling blue, sad
to reserve a table is to book it

explanation.surface: A gloomy instruction to set aside a government paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A blue book is an official government publication, traditionally bound in blue covers, issued by Parliament.

clue.text: Scrap stuff associated with sci-fi novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of the two words are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Rubbish linked with a science-fiction book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a noun for junk beside 'stuff', but it is the verb or noun for a fight; 'novel' is the anagram signal, not the book.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap is a brawl, and fisticuffs means fighting with the fists.

clue.text: Clue — mostly hateful he-men canned feminist analysis

indicators.note: canned is slang for drunk, so these letters are reeling into a new order
mostly means all but the final letter of the word hateful is used

explanation.surface: A hint: macho men, being hateful, are put down by a feminist study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the L from HATEFUL, leaving HATEFU; with CLUE and HEMEN, 'canned' shuffles the fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine Greer's 1970 book is a landmark work of second-wave feminist thought.

clue.text: Get lost mule picked up

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so the word for a mule is said and its sound gives the letters

parts.note: a mule is a backless slipper, a type of shoe

explanation.surface: A command to go away, as a stubborn animal is collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mule' suggests the animal, but it is the backless slipper.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations telling someone or something to go away.

clue.text: Hood of hearse regularly removed in kerfuffles

indicators.note: every second letter of the words Hood of hearse is taken away, keeping the rest

explanation.surface: The top of a funeral car is periodically taken off amid commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hood of hearse' reads as the car's roof, but all three words are the letter string: HOODOFHEARSE, keeping the 1st, 3rd, 5th... letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha and a kerfuffle are both informal words for a fuss or commotion.

clue.text: Think about demoting Germany and Spain — bravo

indicators.note: demoting means moving down; in this down entry the letter for Germany slides lower

parts.note: to dwell on something is to think about it at length
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: A politician considers relegating two European nations, then cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: DWELL ON + E gives DWELLONE; 'demoting' moves its D down to after WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravo and well done are both exclamations of praise for an achievement.

clue.text: Spring evening cut short, almost

parts.note: a spring is a source of water, a well

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is lopped off the word for evening

parts.note: evening here stands for night

explanation.surface: A spring evening ends early, nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring evening' reads as a season, but Spring is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-nigh is an old-fashioned adverb meaning nearly or very nearly.

clue.text: Smack rugby player

definitions.meaning: a smack is a small sailing fishing boat
the front-row forward who hooks the ball back in the scrum

explanation.surface: A blow to a rugby player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a hit or a verb, but it is a type of fishing vessel; a hooker is another.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooker is both a one-masted fishing boat like a smack and a scrum position in rugby.

clue.text: Nick needs spades to break overturned earth

indicators.note: the spade letter breaks into the reversed earth, splitting it open
overturned means the word for earth is turned round, read backwards

parts.note: terra is Latin for earth
S is the abbreviation for spades, the card suit

explanation.surface: A gardener needs a spade to break up dug-over soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' reverses TERRA to ARRET; 'to break' puts S into it, giving ARRE+S+T.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick someone is British slang for apprehending a suspect, as police do.

clue.text: Grip compound securing molar that's lost cap

indicators.note: securing means holding inside, so the enclosure word wraps round the other piece

parts.note: a fold is an enclosure or pen for sheep, a compound

indicators.note: lost cap means the first letter, the top of this down-reading tooth word, is gone

parts.note: a molar is a tooth

explanation.surface: A dental compound holding a molar whose crown has come off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compound' suggests dental filling material, but it is an enclosure for animals; 'that's lost cap' beheads the molar word and 'securing' wraps the pen round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A foothold is a secure place or grip for the foot, or a firm position gained.

clue.text: Oil extracted from skinned sole

indicators.note: skinned means the outer letters are stripped off the word for sole

parts.note: the sole of a foot or shoe is its bottom

explanation.surface: Oil taken from a fish that has been skinned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sole' looks like the fish to be skinned, but it is the bottom of a foot; BOTTOM loses its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, also attar, is a fragrant essential oil distilled from rose petals.

clue.text: Bodyguard intercepting unnamed buddy, causing sorrow

indicators.note: intercepting means cutting in, so the bodyguard letters sit inside the other piece
unnamed means N, the abbreviation for name, is removed

parts.note: a buddy is a companion
SS, the Schutzstaffel, began as Hitler's bodyguard

explanation.surface: A bodyguard blocks an anonymous friend, upsetting him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unnamed' leaves COMPAION; 'intercepting' puts the bodyguard letters inside. Sorrow here is the old sense of sorrowing with another.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassion is pity, fellow-feeling sorrow for another's suffering.

clue.text: Trying giant, clumsy without charm

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the jumbled giant goes round the charm word
clumsy means the letters of giant are put together awkwardly, in a new order

parts.note: to charm or lure someone is to tempt them

explanation.surface: An awkward giant without any charm is wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: 'clumsy' makes ATING, which is split round the charm word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying, as a present participle, means making an attempt at something.

clue.text: Versatile sort of sailor getting sod all after working

parts.note: jack, as in jack tar, is a sailor

indicators.note: working means the letters of sod all after are worked into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A sailor who does nothing once he has a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sod all' (British slang for nothing) looks like the point, but those words with 'after' are the anagram fodder for OFALLTRADES.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack-of-all-trades is a handy person able to turn their hand to many kinds of work.

clue.text: Rogue charged in a dock after taking heroin

indicators.note: in means the word for charged goes inside the other piece
after taking means once the heroin letter has been taken away from the dock word

parts.note: a berth is a ship's place at a dock
H is slang for heroin
to charge is to run at, so charged gives ran

explanation.surface: A defendant charged and in the dock after being caught with heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' and 'dock' call up a courtroom, but dock is a ship's mooring. 'after taking' leaves BERT, and 'in' places the charged word inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogue as an adjective means deviant or out of control, departing from the normal course.

clue.text: Reception from mountain over northern heath

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the mountain word is read backwards

parts.note: Etna is the volcano mountain in Sicily

indicators.note: northern means heading north, upwards in this down entry, so the heath word reads backwards

parts.note: a moor is open heathland

explanation.surface: A greeting from up on a hill above the northern moorland.
explanation.definitionFit: An anteroom is a small waiting room or reception area leading to a larger room.

clue.text: Conviction that number one is positive

definitions.text: Conviction that number one is positive

parts.words: Conviction that number one is positive
parts.note: number one is oneself; feeling sure that you are good is a belief in your own worth

explanation.surface: A belief that the top seed is optimistic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number one' looks like a ranking or a leader, but it means yourself, as in 'look after number one'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is confidence in one's own worth, a positive regard for oneself.

clue.text: Paid for US agent, extremely taken aback when nabbed

indicators.note: nabbed means caught and held, so the reversed piece is held inside the agent word

parts.note: a fed is an FBI agent in US slang

indicators.note: taken aback means the word for extremely is turned back to front

parts.note: too means excessively, extremely

explanation.surface: An FBI man is shocked when arrested and has to pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken aback' looks like surprise but is the reversal signal; 'when nabbed' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To foot the bill means to pay it, so footed is paid for.

clue.text: Dickensian character rejected grand fool

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
git is British slang for a foolish or contemptible person

explanation.surface: A character from Dickens dismisses a grand old idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: Montague Tigg is the swindler in Martin Chuzzlewit.
explanation.definitionFit: Montague Tigg is a confidence trickster in Dickens's novel Martin Chuzzlewit.

clue.text: Dark, unopened icy house, extremely musty

indicators.note: unopened means the opening letter is taken off the ice house word

parts.note: an igloo is a house built of snow and ice

indicators.note: extremely points to the extreme, outermost letters of musty

explanation.surface: A dark, unused, frozen house that smells very stale.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloomy means dim and poorly lit, dark.

clue.text: Bird eaten by black tailless cat somewhere in Kings

indicators.note: eaten by means swallowed, so the bird word goes inside the other letters

parts.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

indicators.note: tailless means the last letter of the cat word is cut off

parts.note: a lynx is a wild cat
a rook is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A bird is devoured by a black cat with no tail in some royal place.
explanation.walkthrough: Kings is Kings County, the New York borough's official county name, not monarchs.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooklyn is coextensive with Kings County in New York State.

clue.text: Barge over national emblem

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the barge word reads upwards in this down entry

parts.note: a keel is a flat-bottomed barge, as used on the Tyne

explanation.surface: A boat capsizes onto a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barge' suggests the verb to shove, but it is a keel, a river barge.
explanation.definitionFit: The leek is a national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day.

clue.text: Fear defeat, ultimately by an own goal

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word defeat

parts.note: an own goal is a blunder, an error

explanation.surface: A footballer dreads losing through scoring against his own side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defeat' looks like the cause of the fear, but only its last letter, T, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is extreme fear or dread.

clue.text: Join by contributing to A Year in Provence

indicators.note: contributing to means going into, so the times sign is put inside the French year

parts.note: in Provence, in France, a year is une année, written ANNEE
by as in multiplied by is written as the times sign, X

explanation.surface: Taking part in Peter Mayle's book about life in southern France.
explanation.walkthrough: A Year in Provence is Peter Mayle's memoir of France; here it is the French word for a year, ANNEE, with X inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To annex is to join or attach, especially territory; annexe is the British spelling.

clue.text: Against having a battle, in the soup

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
the Somme was a First World War battle in 1916

explanation.surface: Being opposed to fighting lands you in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the soup' reads as the idiom for being in trouble; here 'soup' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Consommé is a clear soup made from concentrated stock.
